sense: describing someone or something by a quality: of great courage, of few words, of small build

terms.grammar: the genitive of quality: a noun in the genitive with an adjective, describing another noun
evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.26.3: nōn multī cibī hospitem accipiēs, multī jocī
terms.comment: English “of” with a quality is a genitive in Latin, but only when the quality has an adjective: vir magnī animī, never vir animī (Allen & Greenough §345). It is the regular form for measure, number and age: puer trium annōrum, a boy of three; fossa trium pedum, a three-foot ditch.

terms.grammar: the ablative of quality: a noun in the ablative with an adjective
evidence: Gell. 19.13.2–3: parvā nimis statūrā hominēs; brevī atque humilī corpore hominēs
terms.comment: The ablative does the same work and is the usual case for the body and its looks: parvā statūrā, of small build; caeruleīs oculīs, with blue eyes (Allen & Greenough §415).
A genitive of quality that has become a fixed phrase (see kind).

phrases.latin: nōn multī cibī hospitem accipiēs, multī jocī
phrases.english: you’ll be entertaining a guest of small appetite and plenty of jokes

phrases.latin: nānōs dīcere parvā nimis statūrā hominēs
phrases.english: to call people of very small build “nānī”

sources: The examples are from the Latīnitās loci collections and the note on quantity words, checked there against the texts. The rule is Allen & Greenough’s (§§345, 415).
